title: Likes, dislikes, and invitations
title_target: ชอบไหม ไปกันไหม — Châwp mǎi, pai kan mǎi
goal: Express your tastes, talk about hobbies, and invite people — including how to invite without putting someone on the spot when they'd really rather say no.
bekal: saying you like, don't like, and prefer something

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — Friday afternoon in the office pantry
dialogs.intro: Nok invites Budi and a colleague. Notice how a Thai invitation is built: the word *กัน kan* (together) at the end of the sentence turns a plain statement into an invitation.

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [พี่|Phîi][บูดี|Buu-dii][ชอบ|châwp][ดู|duu][หนัง|nǎng][ไหม|mǎi][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Phi Budi, do you like watching movies?

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ชอบ|Châwp][ครับ|khráp] [แต่|Tàae][ชอบ|châwp][ฟัง|fang][เพลง|phleeng][มากกว่า|mâak-kwàa][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: I do. But I prefer listening to music.
lines.literal: like — (polite). but — like — listen — song — more — (polite).

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [เพลง|Phleeng][แบบ|bàaep][ไหน|nǎi][คะ|khá] [ชอบ|Châwp][เพลง|phleeng][ไทย|thai][ไหม|mǎi][คะ|khá]
lines.id: What kind of music? Do you like Thai songs?
lines.literal: song — kind — which — (polite)? like — song — Thai — (question) — (polite)?

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ชอบ|Châwp][มาก|mâak][ครับ|khráp] [แต่|Tàae][ฟัง|fang][ไม่|mâi][ค่อย|khâwy][ออก|àwk][ครับ|khráp] [เร็ว|Reo][ไป|pai][หน่อย|nàwy][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: I love them. But I can't really catch the words. They're a bit too fast.
lines.literal: like — much — (polite). but — listen — not — very — come-out — (polite). fast — too — a-little — (polite).

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [เย็น|Yen][นี้|níi][มี|mii][คอนเสิร์ต|khawn-sòoet][ค่ะ|khâ] [ไป|Pai][ด้วย|dûai][กัน|kan][ไหม|mǎi][คะ|khá]
lines.id: There's a concert this evening. Want to come along?
lines.literal: evening — this — have — concert — (polite). go — with — together — (question) — (polite)?

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ดี|Dii][เลย|loei][ครับ|khráp] [ที่ไหน|Thîi-nǎi][ครับ|khráp] [แพง|Phaaeng][ไหม|mǎi][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: I'd love to. Where? Is it expensive?

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [ไม่|Mâi][แพง|phaaeng][ค่ะ|khâ] [สาม|Sǎam][ร้อย|ráwy][ค่ะ|khâ] [ชวน|Chuan][พี่|phîi][ต้น|Tôn][ไป|pai][ด้วย|dûai][ไหม|mǎi][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Not expensive. Three hundred. Shall we invite Phi Ton too?
lines.literal: not — expensive — (polite). three — hundred — (polite). invite — older-sibling — Ton — go — too — (question) — (polite)?

lines.speaker: ต้น:
lines.text: [ขอบคุณ|Khàwp-khun][ครับ|khráp] [แต่|Tàae][เย็น|yen][นี้|níi][ไม่ค่อย|mâi-khâwy][สะดวก|sà-dùak][ครับ|khráp] [ไว้|Wái][คราวหน้า|khraao-nâa][นะ|ná][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: Thanks. But this evening isn't very convenient. Next time, okay?
lines.literal: thank-you — (polite). but — evening — this — not-very — convenient — (polite). keep — next-time — okay — (polite).

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [ได้|Dâai][ค่ะ|khâ] [ไม่เป็นไร|Mâi pen rai][ค่ะ|khâ]

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [เจอ|Joee][กัน|kan][กี่|kìi][โมง|moong][ดี|dii][ครับ|khráp] [ผม|Phǒm][อยาก|yàak][กิน|kin][ข้าว|khâao][ก่อน|kàwn][ครับ|khráp]
lines.id: What time's good to meet? I want to eat first.
lines.literal: meet — together — how-many — o'clock — good — (polite)? I — want — eat — rice — first — (polite).

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [หก|Hòk][โมง|moong][ครึ่ง|khrûeng][ค่ะ|khâ] [กิน|Kin][ข้าว|khâao][ด้วย|dûai][กัน|kan][ก็ได้|kâw-dâai][ค่ะ|khâ]
lines.id: Six thirty. We can eat together too.
lines.literal: six — o'clock — half — (polite). eat — rice — with — together — also-can — (polite).

notes: **ชอบ châwp means "like", and it's followed directly by a noun OR a verb** with nothing in between. *ชอบเพลงไทย* (like Thai songs), *ชอบดูหนัง* (like watching movies). There's no "to" or "-ing" as in English "like to watch".

**มากกว่า mâak-kwàa means "more", and it goes at the END.** *ชอบฟังเพลงมากกว่า* (prefer listening to music). To compare two things openly: *ชอบ A มากกว่า B* — *ชอบกาแฟมากกว่าชา* (prefer coffee to tea). Comparison is covered fully in unit 18.
**กัน kan means "together" and turns a sentence into an invitation.** *ไปกันไหม* (shall we go?), *กินข้าวกันไหม* (shall we eat?). The fuller form *ไปด้วยกันไหม* stresses "together".
**ชวน chuan means "to invite".** *ชวนพี่ต้นไปด้วยไหม* = shall we invite Phi Ton too? The word is also used to report being invited: *เขาชวนไปกินข้าว* (they invited me to eat).

**อยาก yàak = want to, and it goes before the verb.** *อยากกินข้าว* (want to eat), *อยากไป* (want to go). ⚠️ To **want a thing**, Thai uses *อยากได้ yàak dâai*: *อยากได้เสื้อใหม่* (want a new shirt). Putting *อยาก* straight in front of a noun sounds broken.

**ฟังไม่ออก fang mâi àwk means "can't make out what you hear".** The pattern *verb + ไม่ออก* means the senses work but the brain doesn't get there: *ดูไม่ออก* (can't tell by looking), *อ่านไม่ออก* (can't read the writing). Compare *ไม่ได้ยิน mâi dâai-yin*, which means you really didn't hear it.

**Notice how Ton declines.** He doesn't say "no"; he says *ไม่ค่อยสะดวก* (not very convenient) and *ไว้คราวหน้านะ* (next time, okay?). This is the standard refusal you met in unit 12 — and Nok accepts it at once without asking why. ⚠️ Asking "why?" after a refusal like this puts the other person on the spot.
**ดีเลย dii loei = "I'd love to, great".** It's the warmest way to accept an invitation. Other common forms: *เอาสิ ao sì* (sure, let's), *ไปสิ pai sì* (let's go).

after: **เฉยๆ *chǒoei-chǒoei* is a very handy answer** when you don't want to praise something but don't want to disappoint either: "so-so". It's far gentler than *ไม่ชอบ*, and Thai people use it all the time.
⚠️ *เกลียด klìat* (hate) sounds much harsher to Thai ears than "hate" does in casual English. For food that doesn't agree with you, use *ไม่ค่อยชอบ* or *กินไม่ได้ kin mâi dâai* (can't eat it).

blocks.text: Notice **เล่น lên** (play), used for games, sports, and instruments: *เล่นกีตาร์* (play guitar). But soccer uses *เตะ tè* (kick) and badminton uses *ตี tii* (hit) — where English simply says "play" for both.

blocks.title: สนุก and สบาย — two words that explain Thailand
items: **สนุก *sà-nùk*** means "fun, enjoyable", and it's one of the values Thai people mention most about themselves. Work, lessons, even meetings — all are expected to have a little *สนุก* in them. The question *สนุกไหม* (was it fun?) is the first response to anyone's holiday story.

**สบาย *sà-baai*** means "comfortable, at ease, carefree". Doubled as *สบายๆ sà-baai-sà-baai*, it means "take it easy, no need to fuss" — and it's the most common answer to almost any question about plans.
These two words stand behind the "laid-back" impression people often describe about Thailand. Using them well makes you sound far closer than perfect grammar ever could.

blocks.title: Who pays
items: In Thailand, **whoever does the inviting usually pays** — and the older person or the higher earner often takes the bill without discussion. Protesting hard only makes things awkward.
A good way to accept is to say thanks and make a promise: *ขอบคุณครับ/ค่ะ คราวหน้าผม/ฉันเลี้ยงนะครับ/คะ* — thank you, next time it's on me.
Among coworkers of the same age, *หารกัน hǎan kan* (splitting the bill) is increasingly common, especially in the city. If in doubt, just ask: *หารกันไหมครับ/คะ*.
